name: Kishkindha Kanda
title: Kishkindha Kanda: Hanuman, Sugriva, Vali and the Search for Sita
description: Read Kishkindha Kanda through Rama’s meeting with Hanuman, the Sugriva–Vali conflict, the search parties, Sampati and Jambavan’s reminder, with sources.
dek: Two men searching for Sita meet another exile. An alliance begins, but friendship will have to survive violence, delay and despair before it can reach the sea.
summary: Kishkindha Kanda brings Rama into alliance with Sugriva through Hanuman. It includes Vali’s death, Sugriva’s restoration, the dispatch of search parties and the southern party’s discovery that Sita is in Lanka. The book ends with Hanuman preparing to cross the ocean after Jambavan recalls his capabilities.
editionNote: References follow Desiraju Hanumanta Rao’s 67-sarga Kishkindha Kanda at ValmikiRamayan.net. The ocean crossing itself begins in Sundara Kanda, although Jambavan’s encouragement belongs here.

sections.heading: Hanuman first approaches as a careful speaker
paragraphs: At Pampa, the beauty of the landscape intensifies Rama’s longing for Sita. Nearby, Sugriva sees two armed strangers and fears they may have been sent by Vali. Hanuman approaches them in an assumed ascetic form to discover who they are and why they have come.

His first achievement is speech. He observes the brothers, asks questions and presents himself without forcing a confrontation. Rama remarks on the quality of his expression. Before Hanuman becomes famous for a leap or a burning city, the narrative establishes his learning and ability to judge an encounter.

Lakshmana explains their situation. Trust begins through the exchange of accurate information, making Hanuman the bridge between people who would otherwise have reasons to fear one another. Our [Hanuman page](/deities/hanuman) follows this combination of intelligence, strength and service.

sections.heading: Rama and Sugriva make a reciprocal promise
paragraphs: Rama and Sugriva establish friendship with a fire as witness. Sugriva can help search for Sita; Rama can help him recover what Vali has taken. The ornaments dropped by Sita give the alliance an immediate emotional reality. Rama handles an object connected with her while still not knowing where she is.

Sugriva explains the feud with his brother. A pursuit into a cave, a long wait and a mistaken conclusion about Vali’s death led to Sugriva’s return and installation. Vali interpreted the events as betrayal, expelled him and took his wife Ruma.

Sugriva needs assurance that Rama can overcome Vali. Demonstrations of strength address that doubt. The alliance is therefore both personal and practical: each party must have confidence that the other can fulfil the promise being made.

sections.heading: Vali’s death remains a disputed act inside the story
paragraphs: Sugriva challenges Vali. In the first combat Rama cannot safely distinguish the brothers and does not shoot; Sugriva returns injured and angry. A distinguishing garland makes a second attempt possible. Tara warns Vali about the changed circumstances, but he goes out to fight.

Rama strikes Vali while the brothers are engaged. Dying, Vali questions the justice of Rama’s intervention and the manner of the attack. Rama answers through arguments about royal authority, punishment and Vali’s conduct toward Sugriva and Ruma.

A careful guide must preserve the objection as well as the answer. The text lets a wounded opponent speak at length. Repeating only Rama’s justification, or only Vali’s accusation, removes the actual structure of the encounter.

sections.heading: Tara and Angada live with the consequences
paragraphs: Tara comes to Vali and laments. Hanuman tries to console her, and Vali gives final instructions concerning Sugriva and Angada. Sugriva’s recovery of power is accompanied by grief and guilt rather than uninterrupted triumph.

The funeral rites give the narrative time to acknowledge the person who has died. Tara worries about Angada’s future in the changed household. Sugriva is installed, and Angada is given the position of heir.

Tara’s role is more than that of a bereaved wife. She has already offered political judgment before the fight, and her ability to interpret people and danger will again matter when Lakshmana arrives in anger.

sections.heading: The rains pass while Rama waits
paragraphs: The rainy season interrupts the search. Rama remains outside the royal city, and descriptions of weather make waiting part of the book’s emotional life. Sugriva enjoys his restored position while Rama remains separated from Sita.

As the season changes, delay becomes a breach of expectation. Hanuman urges Sugriva to act; Rama sends Lakshmana, whose anger threatens to damage the alliance. Tara intervenes and helps make a conversation possible. Sugriva apologizes and gathers the vanara forces.
Friendship here requires maintenance after the first promise. Winning a kingdom does not complete Sugriva’s obligation to the friend whose own loss remains unresolved.

sections.heading: The search becomes a task for an entire network
paragraphs: Sugriva sends parties in four directions. The geographical instructions range across rivers, mountains, regions and extraordinary places. They belong to the epic’s narrative world and should not be treated as a modern survey map with every location securely identified.

The southern party includes Angada, Jambavan and Hanuman. Rama gives Hanuman his ring as a sign that can establish his identity if he finds Sita. This small object will matter as much as physical strength when a frightened captive must decide whether to trust a stranger.

The other parties return without success. The southern search continues through exhaustion and uncertainty. Angada encourages the companions, but the allotted time and the fear of failure press upon them.

sections.heading: Svayamprabha and the danger of giving up
paragraphs: The searchers enter an extraordinary cave and encounter Svayamprabha. Her assistance allows them to leave a place they cannot escape by ordinary means. Survival again depends on receiving help rather than merely overpowering an obstacle.

Once outside, the party confronts the expiry of its deadline. Angada fears the consequences of returning unsuccessfully and considers refusing to return. Hanuman challenges the alternatives before them. The vanaras finally prepare to fast to death.

This is the lowest point of the search. They have travelled, exerted themselves and survived, yet have no usable answer for Rama. The next piece of information arrives when their own account of loss is overheard.

sections.heading: Sampati turns Jatayu’s death into a connection
paragraphs: Sampati hears the searchers speak of Jatayu and learns that his brother has died defending Sita. Their exchange joins the forest narrative to the ocean shore. An act of resistance that seemed to end in failure becomes part of the chain through which Sita can be found.

Sampati identifies Lanka as the place where she is held. He also recounts his own history, including the flight with Jatayu that cost him his wings. The account connects his present knowledge with earlier suffering and a long period of waiting.
The party now has a destination. That solves one problem and exposes another: Lanka lies across an ocean, and knowing where Sita is does not establish who can reach her.

sections.heading: Jambavan reminds Hanuman of his strength
paragraphs: At the shore, the vanaras measure what they can attempt. Some can leap part of the distance; Angada is uncertain about the return journey. Jambavan acknowledges the limits of his own age and turns to Hanuman, who has remained quiet.

In sarga 66 he recalls Hanuman’s birth, childhood and extraordinary capacities. Hanuman responds with renewed confidence and prepares for the crossing. The book ends with that preparation; the leap itself opens Sundara Kanda.

The full childhood curse is narrated in Uttara Kanda 36, not in the same chapter as this speech. Our article [Why Did Hanuman Forget His Powers?](/articles/why-hanuman-forgot-his-powers-jambavan-ramayana) explains the relationship between the two passages. The reminder gives Hanuman no new muscles or weapons. It brings existing capacity into relation with the task that now needs it.

questions.question: Is Jambavan’s speech in Sundara Kanda?
questions.answer: The encouragement is in Kishkindha Kanda 66, with Hanuman’s response and preparations in 67. The actual crossing opens Sundara Kanda.

questions.question: Who tells the search party that Sita is in Lanka?
questions.answer: Sampati, Jatayu’s brother, provides that crucial information after hearing about Jatayu’s death.

questions.question: Why does Rama help Sugriva?
questions.answer: They form a reciprocal alliance. Rama helps address Sugriva’s dispossession, and Sugriva undertakes to help find Sita.
